questions.text: Why is SSH preferred when remotely administering a server?
questions.correctAnswer: SSH encrypts the remote session, including authentication and commands, and provides server authentication and integrity protection. It is preferred over plaintext remote-login protocols because credentials and administrative traffic are not sent openly across the network.
aiRubric: Connects SSH to secure remote administration.
questions.explanation:
SSH is designed for secure remote administration. It protects the traffic between the administrator and the server instead of sending the session as readable network data.

Student note: Remember the contrast: SSH is encrypted; classic Telnet is plaintext.

questions.text: Can Telnet provide a remote interactive terminal similar to SSH?
options: Yes, but classic Telnet does not provide SSH-style encrypted protection
No, Telnet cannot provide a remote terminal
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, but classic Telnet does not provide SSH-style encrypted protection
questions.explanation:
Telnet can provide remote terminal access, but its normal traffic is not encrypted. That is why it should not replace SSH for secure administration.

Student note: The functionality is similar; the security is not.

questions.text: On a Fedora system using systemd, write the command that checks the current status of the OpenSSH server daemon.
questions.explanation:
Fedora manages the OpenSSH server as the `sshd` systemd service. `systemctl status sshd` shows whether it is active and provides recent service information.

Student note: `ssh` is the client command; `sshd` is the server daemon.

questions.text: Write the systemd command that configures the SSH server to start automatically when Fedora boots.
aiRubric: `systemctl enable --now sshd` is also acceptable because it both enables and starts the service.
questions.explanation:
`systemctl enable sshd` configures the service to start at boot. `--now` may be added when you also want it started immediately.

Student note: `start` affects the current session; `enable` controls future boots.

questions.text: Why would an organisation configure Samba on a Linux server?
questions.correctAnswer: Samba lets Linux/Unix systems provide SMB-compatible file and printer sharing and integrate with Windows-style network environments. It can also participate in authentication/domain scenarios depending on the configuration.
aiRubric: Mentions SMB interoperability with Windows clients.
questions.explanation:
Samba is the bridge that lets Linux provide services commonly used by Windows SMB clients.

Student note: The key idea is interoperability: Linux server, SMB/Windows clients.

questions.text: Discuss the main Samba daemons/services and what each one does.
questions.correctAnswer: `smbd` provides SMB file and print services, handles resource locking and authenticates connecting users. `nmbd` provides legacy NetBIOS name/browsing services where those are still required. `winbindd` integrates Windows/AD or NT-domain user and group identities with the local Unix/Linux system. Modern Samba installations may use only the services required by the chosen deployment mode.
aiRubric: Distinguishes file/print service, name/browse service and domain identity integration.
Notes that required services depend on deployment.
questions.explanation:
Samba is not one single background process. Different daemons handle SMB sharing, legacy network naming and domain identity integration.

Student note: Learn the job beside each name: smbd = SMB data/service, nmbd = NetBIOS naming/browsing, winbindd = domain users/groups.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of iptables?
questions.correctAnswer: iptables is a user-space administration tool for configuring, maintaining and inspecting Linux kernel packet-filtering/NAT rule tables. Rules match network packets and apply targets such as ACCEPT, DROP or other processing.
aiRubric: Mentions Linux kernel/netfilter rule tables or equivalent.
Explains that rules decide how matching packets are handled.
questions.explanation:
iptables manages rule tables that control how matching network packets are treated.

Student note: Think rule = match conditions + action/target.

questions.text: Explain the purpose of the iptables `filter`, `mangle` and `raw` tables.
questions.correctAnswer: `filter` is the default table for ordinary packet filtering such as accepting or dropping traffic. `mangle` is for specialised packet alteration/marking. `raw` is processed early and is used mainly for special handling such as configuring connection-tracking exemptions with NOTRACK.
questions.explanation:
iptables has separate tables because different rule types happen at different points and for different purposes.

Student note: filter = permit/block; mangle = alter/mark; raw = early special handling/connection tracking.

questions.text: A web-server log reports that file permissions prevent access. Explain the likely problem.
questions.correctAnswer: The web-server process cannot read or traverse the requested file/directory because Unix file permissions, ownership, ACLs or a parent-directory execute permission do not allow the server account access.
aiRubric: Connects the error to filesystem permissions/ownership/ACLs.
questions.explanation:
Even a correct URL fails when the web-server process cannot read the file or traverse its directory path.

Student note: Check the permissions from the document root all the way to the requested file.

questions.text: A web-server log says the client was denied by server configuration. Explain the likely cause.
questions.correctAnswer: An Apache/httpd access-control rule is denying the request, for example a `Require` rule, directory rule, host/IP restriction or another server configuration directive that rejects that client or location.
aiRubric: Gives a suitable example such as Require/IP/directory rule.
Does not confuse it with simple missing-file error.
questions.explanation:
This message points to web-server access rules rather than ordinary file absence.

Student note: Separate configuration denial from filesystem denial; they are different layers.

questions.text: A web server reports that a directory index is forbidden by rule. What does that normally mean?
questions.correctAnswer: The request targets a directory, no permitted index file is available, and directory listing/index generation is disabled by the server configuration (for example Options -Indexes).
aiRubric: Explains directory request/no usable index file.
Explains that directory listing is disabled.
questions.explanation:
When no index page exists, Apache can either list the directory or forbid that listing. A configuration can deliberately disable directory indexes.

Student note: A missing index file is not always a 404; directory-listing policy also matters.

questions.text: What does a 'premature end of script headers' type web-server error usually indicate?
questions.correctAnswer: A CGI/script process ended, crashed or produced invalid/incomplete HTTP headers before the web server received a valid response header block. Causes can include script errors, wrong interpreter/shebang, permissions or runtime failures.
aiRubric: Explains that the server did not receive valid complete script headers.
Mentions script crash/error or invalid output.
Gives at least one plausible cause.
questions.explanation:
The web server expected valid headers from the script, but the script stopped or produced invalid output first.

Student note: Debug the script itself as well as its interpreter and permissions.

questions.text: How can SELinux cause a Fedora web server to log access errors even when normal Unix permissions appear correct?
questions.correctAnswer: SELinux applies mandatory access-control policy in addition to normal Unix permissions. A file can have readable mode bits but still be blocked because its SELinux type/context or required policy/boolean does not permit the web-server domain to access it. Audit logs and tools such as `ausearch`, `sealert`, `ls -Z` and appropriate relabeling can help diagnose the denial.
aiRubric: Explains SELinux as an additional mandatory-access-control layer.
Explains that normal permissions can look correct while SELinux still blocks access.
questions.explanation:
Fedora may enforce SELinux on top of Unix file permissions. Both layers must permit the access.

Student note: If chmod looks correct but httpd is still denied, check SELinux context and audit logs.
